opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think Minecraft is a really special environment, and I'd argue it's one of the best playgrounds we have for general-purpose agents. The key reason is that Minecraft is open-ended. There's no fixed objective, no single score you're trying to maximize. You spawn into this procedurally generated world, and you can do pretty much anything: you can mine, craft tools, build a house, farm, explore caves, fight the Ender Dragon, or even build working computers out of redstone. That's very different from the classic benchmarks in reinforcement learning, like Atari or Go, where the goal is narrow and well defined.

And that open-endedness is exactly what we want for general agents. In the real world nobody hands you a reward function. You have to decide for yourself what's interesting to do, propose your own tasks, learn new skills, and then build on those skills over time. Minecraft captures a lot of that structure. There's a huge tech tree. You need wood to make a crafting table, the table to make a wooden pickaxe, that to mine stone, and so on up to iron and diamond. So there's a natural curriculum of increasingly complex skills, and an agent has to compose what it already knows to unlock new things.

The other thing that makes Minecraft so valuable is the community. Millions of people play it, and there's an enormous amount of internet-scale data around it: YouTube videos of people playing, wiki pages explaining every recipe and mechanic, Reddit threads with tips and tricks. That was the core idea behind our MineDojo project. Instead of training an agent from scratch in a vacuum, we can tap into all of this human knowledge and use it to learn things like a reward model that understands language and video together, so you can tell the agent "go shear a sheep" and it has some notion of what success looks like.

Then with Voyager we took a different angle. We used a large language model, GPT-4 at the time, as the brain, and had it write code as its action space. The agent proposes its own next task through an automatic curriculum, writes a program to accomplish it, gets feedback from the environment, debugs itself, and when a skill works it gets stored in a skill library it can reuse later. So it's lifelong learning. It keeps exploring and keeps getting better without any human intervention, and it discovered way more items and reached the diamond tool level much faster than prior methods.

So for me, Minecraft isn't really about the game itself. It's a microcosm of the real world that's simple enough to simulate cheaply at scale, yet rich enough that the lessons transfer: open-ended exploration, skill composition, learning from internet knowledge, self-improvement. Those are the same ingredients we need for agents in robotics and in the physical world. I like to think of it as a stepping stone toward what I call a foundation agent, one model that can act across many different worlds, both virtual and real.

r001.rationale: The response says Minecraft has “no fixed objective” and “no single score you're trying to maximize.”

fable-5.1.text:
Minecraft is, to me, one of the most interesting environments ever created for AI, and the reason comes down to one word: open-endedness. Most of the games we've used as AI benchmarks, Go, chess, Atari, even StarCraft, have a very clear objective. You win or you lose, there's a score, and the agent's job is to maximize it. Minecraft has none of that. There's no score. There's no single way to play. You can mine diamonds, you can build a cathedral, you can breed animals, you can fight the Ender Dragon, or you can just wander around and explore. The game gives you an open sandbox and says, go do whatever you want.

That's exactly what makes it a great proxy for the real world. In real life, nobody hands you a reward function. You have to figure out what's worth doing, break it into subgoals, acquire skills, and then compose those skills into something more complex. Minecraft has this beautiful tech tree, where you start by punching trees to get wood, then you craft a table, then a wooden pickaxe, then stone tools, then iron, and eventually diamond. That hierarchy of skills is a miniature version of how a general-purpose agent would have to bootstrap itself in any complex environment.

The other thing I love about it is the data. Minecraft is one of the best-selling games of all time, so there's an enormous amount of human knowledge out there: YouTube tutorials, the Minecraft wiki, Reddit threads where people ask how to do things and other players answer. So we're not training agents in a vacuum. We can give them access to all of that internet-scale knowledge, the same way a new human player would watch a video or look something up. That's what we did with MineDojo, and later with Voyager, where we had a large language model write code as the agent's actions, maintain a growing skill library, and basically teach itself how to get better over time without any human-designed reward.

So I think of Minecraft less as a game and more as a kind of simulated universe, a place where we can study the hard questions about agents: how do you set your own goals, how do you learn continuously, how do you build on what you've already learned. If we can crack those in Minecraft, I think a lot of it transfers to robotics and to real-world agents, which is ultimately where I want this to go.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says Minecraft has “no score” for the agent to maximize.

astra-6.text:
I think of Minecraft as a really interesting sandbox for general-purpose agents because it doesn’t give you just one task to solve. You have to explore, gather resources, craft tools, and build things. And those activities depend on one another. If you want to find diamonds, you first need to figure out how to get the right tools, how to survive, and how to navigate underground. So even a simple goal can require a long sequence of decisions.

What’s particularly interesting is the idea of an agent that keeps developing new skills. It learns how to make a wooden pickaxe, then uses that ability as a building block for something more sophisticated. You want it to accumulate a repertoire of useful behaviors rather than start from scratch every time you give it a new objective.

Minecraft gives you a way to study that in a world that’s much more manageable than the physical world, but still open-ended. It’s not the same as putting a robot in someone’s home, of course. But it’s a useful place to ask: Can an agent explore on its own, learn from feedback, and keep expanding what it can do?

r001.rationale: The response describes Minecraft as open-ended with multiple interdependent activities, but does not state that it has no predefined score to maximize.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Minecraft as a really interesting sandbox for general-purpose agents because it gives you an open-ended world with very simple rules, but an enormous space of things you can do. You can gather resources, build tools, explore, construct buildings. And those activities connect: to accomplish something ambitious, you have to solve a whole sequence of smaller problems.

That changes the question from, “Can an agent solve this particular task?” to, “Can it keep learning and expanding what it knows how to do?” If it discovers how to craft a tool, can it reuse that skill later? If something fails, can it figure out why and try a different approach?

The other interesting part is that there isn’t one finish line. You can give an agent a specific objective, but you can also ask whether it can explore and find useful things to learn on its own. That makes Minecraft a useful setting for studying the combination of planning, memory, exploration, and continual learning that we want in more general agents.

r001.rationale: The response says Minecraft has no single finish line and supports open-ended objectives, but it does not state that there is no predefined score to maximize.
